title: Traffic and Health: Weighing the Evidence
text:
Researchers studying urban air quality have frequently suggested that traffic emissions may contribute to respiratory problems, although the precise magnitude of this effect remains uncertain. Several studies appear to support the link, yet most were conducted in a limited number of cities, which arguably makes their findings difficult to generalise. Those studies, moreover, relied largely on hospital records.

Some commentators go further, claiming that cleaner transport would almost certainly reduce hospital admissions. Such a claim is probably too strong. The evidence suggests a plausible association rather than a proven causal relationship, and the authors themselves describe their conclusions as tentative.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do researchers suggest about traffic emissions?
options: They may contribute to respiratory problems.
They have been proven to cause cancer.
They have no effect on health.
They reduce the number of hospital visits.

questions.text: What do some commentators claim about cleaner transport in the second paragraph?
options: It would almost certainly reduce hospital admissions.
It has already been banned in most cities.

questions.text: What can be inferred about the authors' attitude towards their own conclusions?
options: They are confident that the link is causal.
They present their conclusions as provisional.

questions.text: Why does the writer consider the claim in the second paragraph to be too strong?
options: Because the evidence shows only a plausible association, not proof of causation.
Because cleaner transport is too expensive to implement.
Because hospitals do not keep records.
Because the studies were conducted in many countries.

vocabulary.definition: seeming likely to be true or reasonable, though not proven
to apply findings from specific cases to a wider group
a relationship or link between two things

paragraph_translations: Badacze zajmujący się jakością powietrza w miastach często sugerowali, że emisje z ruchu drogowego mogą przyczyniać się do problemów z oddychaniem, chociaż dokładna skala tego efektu pozostaje niepewna. Kilka badań wydaje się potwierdzać ten związek, jednak większość z nich przeprowadzono w niewielkiej liczbie miast, co zapewne utrudnia uogólnienie ich wyników. Te badania opierały się ponadto w dużej mierze na danych szpitalnych.

Niektórzy komentatorzy idą dalej, twierdząc, że czystszy transport niemal na pewno zmniejszyłby liczbę hospitalizacji. Takie twierdzenie jest prawdopodobnie zbyt mocne. Dane wskazują raczej na prawdopodobny związek niż na udowodnioną zależność przyczynową, a sami autorzy opisują swoje wnioski jako wstępne.
